sources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1002 · physical PDF pp. 58–58

excluded.summaryRead: The assigned problem asks whether a regulation could authorize a future Secretary to define and delimit its ambiguous terms through interpretive rules.
excluded.notesRead:
Assume a regulation states that its ambiguous terms will have the meanings defined and delimited in later interpretive rules issued by the Secretary. The prompt asks whether that instruction would expressly delegate interpretive authority, by analogy to the statutory language acknowledged in Loper Bright. If it did, an agency might preserve something like Auer’s approach by express drafting even if the general presumption were later rejected. (Printed 1002.)

An analysis must identify the source and limits of the agency’s authority to make the first regulation, whether later definitions exercise policy discretion or change binding requirements, which § 553 procedures apply, and what judicial review under § 706 requires. It must also confront the constitutional objection discussed in Decker and Kisor rather than assume that explicit wording cures every problem. The assigned source leaves the hypothetical unresolved; no outcome is recorded as doctrine.

sources.label: Katzmann 50-70(2).pdf · printed pp. 63–64 · physical PDF pp. 14–15

retained.summaryRead: The panel tested the government’s proposed immunity rule by comparing injuries whose differences appeared unrelated to the statute’s purpose.
retained.notesRead:
First compare two pedestrians: a postal driver throws a parcel that strikes one, while the driver’s simultaneous inattention causes the truck to strike the other. Next compare two post-office customers: one slips on liquid spilled from a mishandled parcel and another slips on water negligently left by a janitor. Ask whether the postal-matter exception supplies a reason to immunize one injury in each pair while allowing suit for the other.

The government acknowledged that its reading would distinguish the paired injuries. The panel regarded those distinctions as absurd in context and as a reason to reject that interpretation. These are the judges’ hypothetical examples, not findings about Raila’s accident, and no separate negligence judgment follows from them. A careful answer should tie the anomaly argument to the text, neighboring terms, and overall waiver rather than invoke fairness alone.

edges.label: Bears on
edges.explanation: The hypotheticals are the panel's own test of the government's proposed immunity rule in Raila.

edges.label: Illustrates
edges.explanation: Comparing injuries whose differences have nothing to do with the statute is a way of testing an interpretation by its anomalous results.

retained.title: Study problem: presidential cost priorities and bilingual-education duties
retained.reason: The developed explanation distinguishes discretion within an enacted criterion from presidential substitution of that criterion.

sources.label: lrs-october-1-100(2).pdf · printed pp. 269–270 · physical PDF pp. 25–26

retained.summaryRead: Test the difference between directing a lawful choice and replacing the criterion Congress required.
retained.notesRead:
The classroom hypothetical asks what follows if a bilingual-education statute directs an agency to select the educationally most effective program regardless of expense, while the President directs use of the most cost-effective program regardless of educational efficacy. Start with the enacted criterion and identify the factual or policy discretion it leaves. A supervisory instruction that selects within that discretion differs from an instruction that changes the controlling criterion.

Marbury and Kendall support enforcing a lawful mandatory duty; they do not eliminate the need to identify which choices the statute actually settles. Wirt and Taney expose the further institutional question of who may direct discretion assigned to a subordinate. Sierra Club and the OLC regulatory-review memorandum add the possibility of presidential advice or coordination while preserving the officer’s duty to meet the statute. This is a casebook problem, not a decided case.

edges.label: Explains Ministerial duties, statutory discretion, and the Take Care Clause
edges.explanation: The hypothetical separates discretion left by the education statute from substituting a presidential cost criterion for the mandated efficacy criterion.
edges.classification: explained comparison/application in node and edge context

retained.title: Study problem: can a legislature disclaim the property it creates?
retained.reason: The developed source comparison separates mandatory eligibility, disclaimers, and constitutional procedure, preserving divided Arnett reasoning.

sources.label: lrs-october-100-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 484–487 · physical PDF pp. 55–58

retained.summaryRead: Compare substantive eligibility criteria, a no-entitlement clause, and statutory hearing procedures before deciding whether due process applies.
retained.notesRead:
The notes ask whether a legislature can prescribe mandatory eligibility criteria while declaring that the law creates no property interest under the Fourteenth Amendment. Identify first whether the operative criteria actually confine administrative discretion. Then determine what the disclaimer is about: unconditional receipt, conditional program funding, or the constitutional effect of individually enforceable eligibility standards.

Barry found no mandatory shelter entitlement and therefore did not need to give the disclaimer independent effect. Weston found mandatory welfare rights and interpreted the federal disclaimer in context. Arnett then presents a distinct question: may a legislature define the substantive right as including only the procedural protections it chose? Rehnquist’s plurality answered in that direction; Powell and Blackmun, joined in rejecting that rationale by the dissenters, treated constitutional procedure as an independent guarantee. These are questions for comparing sources, not a categorical assertion that every disclaimer succeeds or fails.

edges.label: Explains From the right–privilege distinction to claims of entitlement
edges.explanation: The problem compares operative limits on discretion, disclaimer language, and procedural provisions to identify the asserted entitlement.

retained.title: Study problem: a defective record after Vermont Yankee
retained.reason: It explains the Vermont Yankee distinction between actual failure of support and a preference for extra procedures, with two substantive relations.

sources.label: lrs-october-100-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 702–706 · physical PDF pp. 124–128

retained.summaryRead: A challenger must distinguish an actual defect in a rule’s evidentiary justification from a preference for additional procedures that might reveal a defect.
retained.notesRead:
Assume participants wanted cross-examination of a technical study and the agency refused. One proposed argument is that a better hearing might have produced a better record. Another identifies a concrete unresolved flaw in the study that leaves the final rule inadequately supported. The notes ask how these arguments differ after Vermont Yankee.

The decision bars courts from routinely adding preferred procedural devices to § 553, but leaves review of the rule’s justification intact. The substantive argument therefore requires identifying a real deficiency, while an abstract demand for extra procedures may only hypothesize one. Nova Scotia and American Radio Relay raise the adjacent question whether disclosing the critical study is already part of statutory meaningful comment. Kavanaugh and Levin offer opposing accounts of that interpretive boundary. This is a casebook problem, not a decided case.

edges.label: Explains Disclosure of studies, the administrative record, and significant comments
edges.explanation: The exercise asks for a concrete failure of support rather than speculation that more process might expose one.

retained.summaryRead: The assigned notes ask how courts should distinguish shared constitutional grievances from statutory informational injuries.
retained.notesRead:
The casebook asks why a Black housing tester’s statutory right to truthful information supports a claim while a citizen’s interest in CIA-budget information under a constitutional provision did not support Richardson’s suit. It also compares contractors’ equal opportunity to compete with a taxpayer’s interest in an informed electoral process. Analyze the interest asserted, the relevant text, the claimant’s relation to it, and whether Congress expressly authorized review.

A second question follows Sunstein’s discussion: if Congress can create an enforceable informational interest, how far can it recognize interests in preservation of distant landscapes or endangered species? State Sunstein’s argument and then test it against the assigned TransUnion and Spokeo limits. The notes frame this as a disputed question.

retained.title: Study questions: What work does special solicitude do?
retained.reason: It compares the different Massachusetts rationales with later state suits rather than supplying a floating scenario.

sources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1239–1243 · physical PDF pp. 155–159

retained.summaryRead: The notes ask whether Massachusetts rests on a procedural right, property injury, increased risk, or sovereign status, and how each explanation changes the rule’s reach.
retained.notesRead:
Identify each possible basis in Massachusetts: the state’s ownership of coastal land, the sovereign powers displaced by the Union, the statutory route for review of a rulemaking petition, and a reduction in future climate risk. Explain what each contributes to injury, causation, or redressability. Then assess Roberts’s objection that the remedy must address the particular land injury actually identified.

Use the assigned later cases to test the proposed rule. California v. Texas rejects an unsupported causal link; United States v. Texas distinguishes enforcement discretion; Biden v. Nebraska divides over the relationship between a state and its instrumentality. Explain which reading of Massachusetts survives each comparison.

edges.label: Explains State plaintiffs and special solicitude
edges.explanation: Different rationales produce different limits for later state suits.

retained.title: Study questions: How broadly should the statutory interest be defined?
retained.reason: It preserves the competing descriptions of NCUA’s protected interest and explains their effect on the zone inquiry.

sources.label: lrs-november-165-end(2).pdf · printed pp. 1253–1259 · physical PDF pp. 163–169

retained.summaryRead: Compare NCUA’s market-limitation rationale with the dissent’s concern that incidental benefits would erase the zone-of-interests requirement.
retained.notesRead:
NCUA identifies an interest in limiting credit-union customer markets. Its dissent identifies the provision’s internal cooperative and financial-stability purposes. Explain why the chosen level of description matters and what evidence in the statutory text and operation supports each account.

Apply both approaches to Air Courier’s postal employees, the hypothetical stenographer harmed by omitted on-the-record hearings, and Twin Rivers’s paper companies. Then explain why Thompson and Patchak satisfied the test under the supplied descriptions. Distinguish injury in fact from membership in the statutory zone at every step.
